fullPassage: Covering the president has become an industry unto itself. Hundreds of "beat reporters" - journalists who cover the White House on a daily basis - work from the basement of the White House. Twice a day, these reporters meet with the president's press secretary to get a briefing on the day's activities. Television cameras covering these briefings have been a frequent source of conflict between the press secretary and the press, as some journalists use these press briefings as an opportunity to grandstand for the cameras. Typically, the press is on call twenty-four hours a day, unless the press secretary puts a "lid" on the news, which means that no big announcements are planned. Most presidents have "feuded" with particular journalists and publications at one time or another. Richard Nixon disliked the Washington Post and New York Times, and had his vice president publicly attack them. The Clinton White House singled out Sue Schmidt of the Washington Post as a reporter with a vendetta against the president. President George W. Bush publicly used a rude word to describe New York Times reporter Adam Clymer, a sentiment that Vice President Cheney agreed with. President Kennedy, on the other hand, enjoyed a friendly relationship with the press corps, partly because he singled out favorites for special treatment in return for favorable coverage. In spite of the tension between the president and the press corps, the two have a symbiotic relationship. The president needs the press to deliver his message, and the press needs access to the president in order to do its job. It's not uncommon for White House staffers to leak information to select journalists in order to shape the coverage. Sometimes the president will grant exclusive interviews to certain reporters as a way to dominate the headlines.

questions.stem:
다음 주어진 글 다음에 이어질 글의 순서로 가장 적절한 것을 고르시오.

Most presidents have "feuded" with particular journalists and publications at one time or another.

(A) President George W. Bush publicly used a rude word to describe New York Times reporter Adam Clymer, a sentiment that Vice President Cheney agreed with. President Kennedy, on the other hand, enjoyed a friendly relationship with the press corps, partly because he singled out favorites for special treatment in return for favorable coverage.

(B) In spite of the tension between the president and the press corps, the two have a symbiotic relationship. The president needs the press to deliver his message, and the press needs access to the president in order to do its job.

(C) Richard Nixon disliked the Washington Post and New York Times, and had his vice president publicly attack them. The Clinton White House singled out Sue Schmidt of the Washington Post as a reporter with a vendetta against the president.

det.korean: 대통령들은 특정 언론·기자와 종종 반목했다. (C) 닉슨은 워싱턴포스트·뉴욕타임스를 싫어했고 클린턴 백악관은 수 슈미트를 원한을 가진 기자로 지목했다. (A) 부시는 뉴욕타임스 기자에게 무례한 말을 했고(체니도 동의), 반대로 케네디는 특정 기자를 편애하며 언론과 우호적으로 지냈다. (B) 이런 긴장에도 불구하고 대통령과 언론은 서로를 필요로 하는 공생 관계를 맺는다.
det.analysis:
① (A)-(B)-(C) ❌: 결론(B, '그 긴장에도 불구하고')이 구체적 긴장 사례(C,A)보다 먼저 나오면 무엇에 대한 결론인지 알 수 없다.

② (A)-(C)-(B) ❌: (A)가 먼저 나오면 부시·케네디 사례가 앞선 반목 사례 없이 갑자기 등장해 'on the other hand'의 대조 대상이 불명확해진다.

③ (C)-(A)-(B) ✅: 도입문의 '반목했다'를 구체화하는 닉슨·클린턴 사례(C)가 먼저 나오고, 이어 부시의 사례와 대조적으로 우호적이었던 케네디 사례(A)가 나온 뒤, 이 모든 사례에도 '불구하고' 공생 관계라는 결론(B)으로 마무리되는 것이 가장 자연스럽다 ←정답

④ (B)-(C)-(A) ❌: 결론(B)이 가장 먼저 나오면 아직 제시되지 않은 긴장 사례를 전제로 결론을 내리는 셈이라 흐름이 끊긴다.
det.tip: 지시어·연결어 확인: (A)의 'on the other hand'는 앞선 부정적 사례가 필요, (B)의 'In spite of the tension'은 긴장 사례가 모두 제시된 후에 와야 함

Typically, the press is on call twenty-four hours a day, unless the press secretary puts a "lid" on the news, which means that no big announcements are planned. Most presidents have "feuded" with particular journalists and publications at one time or another. ①Richard Nixon disliked the Washington Post and New York Times, and had his vice president publicly attack them. ②The Clinton White House singled out Sue Schmidt of the Washington Post as a reporter with a vendetta against the president. ③President George W. Bush publicly used a rude word to describe New York Times reporter Adam Clymer, a sentiment that Vice President Cheney agreed with. ④Many young journalists today dream of someday opening their own small restaurant near Capitol Hill. President Kennedy, on the other hand, enjoyed a friendly relationship with the press corps, partly because he singled out favorites for special treatment in return for favorable coverage. In spite of the tension between the president and the press corps, the two have a symbiotic relationship. The president needs the press to deliver his message, and the press needs access to the president in order to do its job. It's not uncommon for White House staffers to leak information to select journalists in order to shape the coverage. Sometimes the president will grant exclusive interviews to certain reporters as a way to dominate the headlines.
